content: 1. The report must be reviewed by the individual responsible for overseeing the facility. This ensures that all data and processes align with the required standards and protocols. 2. The facility supervisor or the person in charge is tasked with reviewing the reports to ensure accuracy and completeness. 3. If any issues or discrepancies are identified in the report, the person in charge will provide feedback to the responsible individual. This feedback will guide the necessary corrections to client-level data. 4. Reports and data can be utilized by the facility supervisor or staff at various stages of the business process, whether during earlier steps, at the current stage, or even outside the business process. This can be automated and performed digitally. 5. Depending on local policies, active submission of data may not be required. Instead, district-, provincial-, and national-level Ministries of Health (MOH) may directly access the data for reporting purposes. 6. Submitted data should be reviewed to assess progress and make informed decisions regarding improvements and necessary actions. 7. After reviewing the data, it is essential to determine whether any feedback is required. 8. If feedback is necessary, the focal person will communicate this to the facility. In cases of errors, the facility may need to restart the process and resubmit the corrected data. 9. Adapting workflows requires further validation through interviews with targeted personas or by observing their work. This helps identify differences that need to be reflected in the digital system. 10. The WHO Handbook for digitalizing primary healthcare provides guidance for developing new workflows or revising existing ones. 11. Core data elements are outlined to support decision-making logic, populate indicators, and measure performance metrics. A comprehensive data dictionary, including input options, calculations, validation checks, and standardized terminology codes (e.g., ICD, SNOMED), is available in Web Annex A. 12. The core data elements are considered 80% generic, with the expectation that the remaining 20% will be adapted to the specific country context. 13. Health workers should check for danger signs before each contact. If danger signs are present, the woman should be urgently referred to a hospital. If no danger signs are present, the normal contact process should continue. 14. Decision-support logic and algorithms are deconstructed from WHO ANC guidelines into a format that clearly defines inputs, outputs, and required actions. These are operationalized in a digital decision-support system. 15. Decision-support tables use an adaptation of the Decision Model Notation (DMN) format, which reflects IF/THEN statements to guide clinical decisions. 16. Decision trees can supplement decision-support tables by visualizing pathways, especially for decision points with multiple inputs and outputs. 17. Scheduling logic is essential for digital tracking of clients to ensure timely provision of services according to clinical protocols. This includes mapping schedules for upcoming contacts, immunizations, and lab tests. 18. Indicators and performance metrics are aggregated from core data elements and align with the WHO ANC monitoring framework and WHO-UNICEF guidance. These indicators can be automatically populated into a digital Health Management Information System (HMIS), such as DHIS2. 19. WHO does not recommend universal screening for intimate partner violence (IPV) but encourages healthcare providers to address the topic with women who present injuries or conditions potentially related to violence. Specific protocols, training, confidentiality measures, and referral systems must be in place for this to be implemented effectively. 20. The availability of functional ultrasound machines and trained health workers at healthcare facilities is critical for providing comprehensive antenatal care. 21. Decision-support logic includes concrete actions based on clinical data, such as referrals, treatments, or counseling. These actions are guided by IF/THEN statements and supported by annotations or pop-up alerts for health workers. 22. Scheduling logic ensures that health workers are aware of the timing for the next client contact, based on recommendations for eight scheduled contacts throughout pregnancy. 23. Indicators such as the percentage of pregnant women receiving oral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) or HIV counseling and testing during pregnancy are tracked to monitor program performance and outcomes. 24. The transition from paper-based forms to digital systems may require reflection on whether existing data elements should be incorporated into the digital system. This process should be customized based on national guidelines and local context.
